blocks.html:
You post an announcement. By Thursday, three people have done the thing and four haven't — and two of the four thought they had.

Your post was clear about the change. It said what was moving, when, and why. What it never said was what you wanted anyone to do about it, so each reader answered that question themselves: one assumed it started immediately, one assumed it was background, one decided to wait and see.

The gap wasn't writing. It was labelling — telling people, before they read a word, whether this message asks something of them. That one bracket at the front of a subject line is the difference between a message that lands and one you spend a week chasing.

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to:

  1. Label any message Action Needed or Informed, correctly, from the reader's point of view.
  2. Choose the channel that makes the label work — post, chat, email, Headline or #Events.
  3. Split a message that is genuinely both, instead of sending one long thing that buries the action.

About 15 minutes. Keep Ninety.io open in another tab — the task at the end uses it.

The same announcement, two ways

Without a labelLabelled
The message“Timesheets are moving to the new system from Monday.”“[ACTION NEEDED] Timesheets move to the new system Monday — submit this week's hours in the old one by Friday 5pm.”
What each reader doesDecides for themselves whether it's a task or a fact. Most decide “later”.Knows within two words that there's something to do, and what it is.
By ThursdayThree done, four not, two of whom thought this didn't apply to them.Anyone who hasn't acted knows they haven't acted.
Your weekChasing individuals, re-explaining, one awkward conversation.One reminder in the same thread, to everyone, visible to everyone.

The label does one job: it tells the reader what kind of message this is before they decide whether to engage. Everything else in this lesson is about making sure the label is accurate and that the channel can carry it.

Step 1: Action Needed or Informed?

The test is about the reader, not the sender: does someone have to do something differently because of this?

  • [ACTION NEEDED] — someone must do something: complete a task, change a habit, update a system, adopt a new process. It's a baseline expectation, not a suggestion.
  • [INFORMED] — no action required. Awareness: policy background, context, where the firm is heading.
Every communication gets the tag, at the start of the subject line or post title: [ACTION NEEDED] or [INFORMED]. If a message arrives without one, ask the sender which it is — don't guess, and don't assume the safe answer.

The commonest mistake is tagging something Action Needed “to be safe” when nobody has to act. That trains people to ignore the tag, and then the real ones stop working.

Step 2: Choose the channel

Ask: does this need a record, a response, or a meeting?

ChannelForNot for
Outlook emailExternal parties; anything needing a formal record or paper trail; formal decisions; firm-wide announcements that require acknowledgmentInternal project coordination, quick internal questions
Teams channel postInternal group work, project discussion, day-to-day decisions, a request for a colleague to actClient communication, firm-wide announcements
Teams private chatA quick question to one or two peopleAnything a third person will need later
Ninety.io HeadlineItems for the whole firm at the all-team meeting: wins, alignment, questions that deserve discussionUrgent same-day requests, detailed explanations
#EventsUpcoming events: training, gatherings, internal deadlinesAnnouncements that aren't events
The HubApproved, finished reference materialAnything in progress (Lesson 5)

Posting a Ninety.io Headline

Headlines go to the all-team meeting. A headline is a prompt for discussion, not the full explanation — one or two lines, tagged, and enough for someone to know whether to ask you about it.

  1. Open the relevant meeting agenda in Ninety.io.
  2. Find the Headlines section for that meeting.
  3. Click + Add Headline.
  4. Paste your headline with the tag at the start.
  5. Save. It appears on the next meeting's agenda.

Example: [INFORMED] Closed the Redfern engagement two weeks early — client asked about a follow-on. Happy to walk through what worked.

Events

Post upcoming events in #Events. If it also needs the firm's attention — a training that changes how people work, say — the announcement goes wherever the action belongs and the event still goes in #Events.

blocks.prompt: “Starting Monday, all timesheets must be submitted by 5pm Friday.” How do you label it?
options: Neither — it's a fact about the system
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. People have to do something differently, so it's Action Needed.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Someone has to change what they do, which makes it [ACTION NEEDED]. The change of date is the action, not the news.

blocks.prompt: “Here's the background on why we moved to a new CRM.” How do you label it?
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Context with nothing to do is Informed — and tagging it Action Needed would weaken every real one.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: It's background with no action, so [INFORMED]. “To be safe” is how a tag stops meaning anything.

blocks.prompt: A policy change needs every person to formally acknowledge they've read it. Where does it go?
options: A Teams private chat to each person
A reaction on a channel post
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. A firm-wide acknowledgment needs a record of who was told, and that's email.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: An acknowledgment on record is a formal record, so it's email — labelled [ACTION NEEDED].

blocks.prompt: You want the firm to recognise a win at the all-team meeting. Where does it go?
options: A private chat with your manager
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Yes — a short tagged Headline, and a reaction in #Wins if you want to celebrate it there too.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Wins for the all-team meeting go in a Ninety.io Headline. Email would reach everyone but wouldn't put it on the agenda.

blocks.promptHtml:
You found a client-onboarding shortcut that cut setup time in half. You want the whole team to know about it and start using it.

Decide how you'd share it, how you'd label it, and draft the actual Headline text.
rubric: Labels it [ACTION NEEDED], because people are being asked to adopt it — and says what adopting it means in practice
Chooses a Ninety.io Headline to raise it at the all-team meeting, rather than a firm-wide email
Drafts a Headline that is short, starts with the tag, and prompts discussion rather than explaining everything
Names a fitting place for the detail — a #Lessons post with the steps, so the Headline doesn't have to carry them
Says how they'll know it's been adopted, rather than assuming the announcement is the change
blocks.coachContext: Every message is labelled [ACTION NEEDED] or [INFORMED], with the tag at the start of the subject line or post title, decided from the reader's point of view. A method people should adopt is [ACTION NEEDED]. A win or an alignment point for the whole firm goes in a Ninety.io Headline for the all-team meeting: short, tagged, a prompt for discussion. Detail belongs in a #Lessons post. Adoption needs a way of noticing whether it happened. No prices.

blocks.promptHtml:
Different conditions: this message is genuinely both.

OneAccord is changing how engagement status is reported. You need every engagement lead to update their status by Thursday and you want the firm to understand why the change is happening, because it came out of a client conversation that matters to how people sell.

One long email would carry both. What do you actually send, in what order, and why is one message the wrong answer?
rubric: Sends the [ACTION NEEDED] message to the people who must act — engagement leads — in the channel or mail that will get it done, with the deadline and what updated means
Sends or posts the [INFORMED] part for the wider firm — the reason behind the change — separately, so it isn't buried under a task
Keeps the two audiences and two purposes separate rather than one long email that is half instruction and half context
Explains why splitting matters: an action buried in context gets missed, and context attached to a task reads as spin
Uses the all-team meeting or a Headline for the alignment part if it deserves discussion, and says which they'd choose
blocks.coachContext: A message with two purposes gets split: the [ACTION NEEDED] part goes to the people who must act, with a clear deadline and definition of done; the [INFORMED] part goes to the wider audience for alignment, where it won't be buried under a task. One combined email makes the action easy to miss and the context read as justification. Alignment that deserves discussion can also go to the all-team meeting as a Headline. No prices.

blocks.prompt: A message arrives asking you to do something, and it has no tag. What do you do?
options: Ask the sender which it is
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. Ask the sender — guessing either way is how the wrong thing gets done, or the right thing doesn't.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Ask the sender. Assuming Informed loses the action; assuming Action Needed floods everyone with false alarms.

blocks.label: In Ninety.io
blocks.instructions:
Two minutes, on a real item:
  • Find something worth telling the firm — a win, something you learned that others would sell better for knowing, or a question that deserves ten minutes at the all-team meeting.
  • Write the Headline. One or two lines, tag first. If you can't get it under three lines, the detail belongs somewhere else — a #Lessons post, probably.
  • Add it to the Headlines section of the next meeting agenda.

If you genuinely have nothing this week, take the last Headline you read and rewrite it as you would have written it — then note what you'd have cut.
